questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Basis Using a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070092/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
questions.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070092/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 8 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 5-3\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 3 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 3 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 3 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070092/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 5-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 9 \\ -2 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to the Standard Basis
questions.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070092/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 1-1\cdot 6}[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 9 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
